facts: This is an appeal by special leave against the judgment of the High Court of Patna which allowed an appeal against the acquittal of the appellants and convicted hem to life imprisonment for an offence u/s. 302 read with S. 149 of the Indian Penal Code.

Nineteen persons were committed by the Munsif Magistrate of Banka, District Bhagalpur to take their trial before the Sessions Court of offences u/s. 148 and S. 302 read with S. 149 of the Indian Penal Code.
One of them, Jyotish Mandal was murdered before the Sessions trial.
The order 18 were acquitted by the learned Sessions Judge of Bhagalpur.
On an appeal by the State against this acquittal the four appellants were sentenced as above mentioned.
Ram Prasad Mandal and Dasrath Mandal had gone to Sambhuganj in order to collect the salary of Dasrath Mandal.
P.W. 2, Bhagwan Mandal was also alleged to have accompanied them.

Their brother, Sheonandan Mandal, P.W. 1 lodged a complaint at 2 a.m. on July 14, 1965, at the Sambhuganj police station to the following effect : His brothers and Bhubneshwar Mandal did not return even after one hour of night fall, he and his relations Davendra Mandal and Mahendra Mandal and Bibekanand Mandal were waiting for them in their 'bathan'.
At about 8.30 p.m. he heard a hulla in the 'Bahiyar' in the western side "Dauro ho jan gailo" twice and recognised the voice to be that of his brother Ram Prasad Mandal.
He then took a torch, lathi, bhala and along with Davendra Mandal and Bibekanand Mandal and Ambika Mandal ran towards west raising hulla.
issues: The powers of the High Court in an appeal against acquittal.
The principles laid down in Sheo Swarup's case (supra) afford a correct guide for the appellate court's approach to a case in disposing of such an appeal; and

The different phraseology used in the judgments of this Court, such as, '(i) 'substantial and compelling reasons', (ii) 'good and sufficiently cogent reasons', and (iii)'strong reasons' are not intended to curtail the undoubted power of an appellate court in an appeal against acquittal to review the entire evidence and to come to its own conclusion; but

The doubt should, however, be reasonable and as observed recently by this Court, the doubt should be such which rational thinking men will reasonably, honestly and conscientiously entertain and not the doubt of a timid mind which fights shy - though unwittingly it may be or in afraid of the logical consequences, if that benefit was not given.
petitioner_arguments: The defence of the accused was that Gaibi Mandal, father of Jyotish Mandal (who was himself murdered after the committal and before the Sessions trial) had been murdered in the month of January, 1965, and in that case the two deceased persons, Ram Prasad Mandal and Dasrath Mandal as also P.W. 3 Mahendra Mandal, and P.W. 4 Ambika Mandal were standing their trial for that murder.

Some of the accused persons in this case, including two of the appellants Jagdish Mandal and Bhubneshwar Mandal were the prosecuting witnesses in the Gaibi murder case and they have, therefore, been falsely implicated by the informant, the brother of Ram Prasad Mandal and Dasrath Mandal.
respondent_arguments: The prosecution witnesses 1, 3, 6, and 10 are members of the family of the deceased.
P.W. 2 does not seem to be an independent or dis-interested witness.

That he was not a disinterested witness is also seen from the fact that Bhubneshwar Mandal and Eknath Mandal are, according to him, said to have talked with him about a compromise of the proceedings under Section 144, Cr.P.C. when he had gone to Sambhuganj to show the 'Kebala' etc. to the Sub-Inspector in the case under Section 144, Cr.P.C.
court_reasoning: The learned Judges of the High Court have ignored very important points in the evidence in the case and allowed the appeal against acquittal and convicted the present appellants.
We do not consider it necessary to refer to all the latter decision on this subject except the latest one in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Samman Dass, 1972 Indlaw SC 673 to the following effect :

The doubt should, however, be reasonable and as observed recently by this Court, the doubt should be such which rational thinking men will reasonably, honestly and conscientiously entertain and not the doubt of a timid mind which fights shy - though unwittingly it may be or in afraid of the logical consequences, if that benefit was not given.
holding: The final decision is not provided in this text.
